context.text: 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is gradually added to 25.0 cm³ of 0.180 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid. Ethanoic acid: pKₐ = 4.76. Complete the pH curve and select a suitable indicator. Round pH to 0.1; volume snaps to 0.5 cm³. Assume 25 °C and additive volumes.

prompt.text: Choose both curve sections, set initial and final pH and equivalence volume, then select an indicator.

scaffolds.purpose: Original curve-construction conventions and indicator transition ranges.

content.text: Drag the three anchors or use the numeric controls. pH steps are 0.1; volume steps are 0.5 cm³. The joining pH is calculated from the selected acid/base species. Equivalence means equal acid/base equivalents; an indicator end-point is its observed colour change.
Find moles of acid/base equivalents first. Before equivalence consider the starting reagent and any buffer; after equivalence consider the added reagent and the total mixed volume.

workedAnswer.text: On smaller screens, swipe the model graph horizontally to inspect its full axis and final pH.

workedAnswer.alt: Checked titration curve with source-equilibrium shape and all three numerical anchors.

workedAnswer.text: Initial pH 2.8; equivalence 22.5 cm³ (pH 8.9); final pH 12.9.
ethanoic acid requires the weak acid section, rising.
The added sodium hydroxide requires the strong base section.
Use [H⁺] ≈ √(Kₐ × c). Rounded initial pH = 2.8.
Match H⁺ and OH⁻ equivalents: V = (25 × 0.18 × 1) ÷ (0.2 × 1) = 22.5 cm³.

The curve uses charge balance, weak-species equilibrium and Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C with ideal concentrations and additive volumes. A weak-acid buffer before equivalence has acid and conjugate base; added weak titrant after equivalence may form a buffer. Diprotic cases use the question’s stated complete-dissociation model.
